svg.aria-label: Diagram: rules for dynamic membership groups in Microsoft Entra ID, showing the single-expression anatomy and the ceilings of 3072 characters, five expressions in the rule builder and 15000 dynamic groups per tenant, the operator precedence order that makes -and bind tighter than -or, the fact that a change to any attribute reprocesses every rule in the organization, and the chain that makes group membership only as strong as write permissions on the attributes the rule references
svg.title: A dynamic membership rule is a program that ships straight to production and runs on every attribute change in the directory
svg.text: A membership rule is code. There is no staging directory to test it in.
It runs against every user and device you have, re-runs whenever any attribute anywhere changes, and you cannot correct its output by hand.
The anatomy, and the three ceilings
user.department -eq “Sales”
— <Property> <Operator> <Value>. Property names are case sensitive; values are not.
3,072 characters
the total length of the body of your membership rule — the real complexity ceiling
5 expressions
all the rule builder supports. Past that, the text box — and device rules are text box only
15,000 groups
the maximum number of dynamic membership groups in a single tenant
Operator precedence, highest to lowest — and the line where rules go wrong
-eq -ne -startsWith -notStartsWith -contains -notContains -match -notMatch -in -notIn
-not
-and
-or
-any -all
-and binds tighter than -or.
So a rule meant as “US staff in Marketing or Sales” silently becomes
“(US and Marketing) or (anyone in Sales, anywhere)” without parentheses.
It parses. It saves. It populates. Nothing reports a problem.
What runs, and when
“When an attribute changes for a user or device, all
rules for dynamic membership groups in the
organization are processed for changes.”
Not just your rule. Every rule in the tenant.
And rules “evaluate every user and device in your
tenant, including objects that are inactive or no
longer in use” — stale objects inflate membership
and slow processing, so clean up before you build.
Processing time is a shared tenant resource.
The chain that decides who is in the group
“The security of that group’s membership depends on
who can modify the attributes referenced in the rule.”
“The security of that access is only as strong as the
write controls on the attributes in the rule.”
Watch on-premises attributes especially: some “might
be configured with permissions that allow users to
modify their own values (SELF write).”
This is why role-assignable groups ban dynamic
membership outright — post #32.
Two rules that behave unlike the rest, and the status you have instead of a test run
The two special cases
Direct Reports for “{objectId}”
The manager is also added to the group. Only direct
reports, never their reports. And it “can’t be combined
with any other membership rules” — an island.
user.objectId -ne null
“All users” — and it “adds business-to-business guest
users and member users”. Add a userType test to exclude.
Six states, and no way to preview
Evaluating · Processing · Update complete · Not started
Processing error · Update paused
You cannot dry-run a rule. You save it, and then read
the status to find out what it did.
A Groups Administrator can pause processing. If nothing
in the whole organization processes for over 24 hours,
an alert appears above All groups.
Sources: Manage rules for dynamic membership groups, and Create or edit a dynamic membership group and get its processing status, on Microsoft Learn.
